JOB APPLICANT RECORD RETENTION REQUIREMENTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS JOB APPLICANT RECORD RETENTION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory record-retention requirements for job application materials, resumes, and related hiring records -- for applicants Acme, Inc. hires and applicants Acme, Inc. does not hire alike -- together with the shorter federal baseline those requirements exceed. It reflects Acme, Inc.'s record-retention policy for this category of records as of October 1, 2026. It states facts about what California and federal law require; it does not itself determine that any specific record must be retained or destroyed on any particular date, and it does not tell Acme, Inc. what to do about any specific record, applicant, employee, subpoena, litigation hold, or pending charge, complaint, or lawsuit -- circumstances like those can extend the time before which a record covered by this document may be destroyed, beyond the general periods described here.

CALIFORNIA'S FOUR-YEAR RETENTION REQUIREMENT FOR APPLICANT AND EMPLOYMENT RECORDS
Government Code § 12946(a), part of the Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), makes it an unlawful practice for an employer, labor organization, or employment agency subject to FEHA -- including Acme, Inc. -- to fail to maintain and preserve applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, and separately makes it unlawful for an employer to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum of four years after the date of the employment action taken. That reaches both a hired applicant's personnel file and a rejected applicant's application materials. This four-year duration took effect January 1, 2022. Before that date the statute required only two years; the current four-year period was enacted by 2021 legislation, Stats. 2021, ch. 278 (SB 807), whose Legislative Counsel's Digest describes the change as increasing "the above-described records and files retention requirement from 2 years to 4 years."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be an unlawful practice for employers, labor organizations, and employment agencies subject to the provisions of this part to fail to maintain and preserve any and all applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum period of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, or for employers to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum period of four years after the date of the employment action taken."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12946.)
  "This bill would increase the above-described records and files retention requirement from 2 years to 4 years and would delete the exemption of the State Personnel Board, thus requiring the board to retain these records for 4 years."
  — Legislative Counsel's Digest, Cal. SB 807 (2021-2022 Reg. Sess.) (Stats. 2021, ch. 278) (California Legislative Information text), Legislative Counsel's Digest, SB 807 (2021) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202120220SB807)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. The Legislative Counsel's Digest is part of the same 2021 enactment as the statute itself (the bill that produced the current text of § 12946), so it is disclosed here as part of the same source rather than as a fully independent second authority; it is quoted because it is the clearest primary-source statement of the prior (2-year) duration and the reason the period changed, a fact the current statutory text alone does not state. The statute's four-year clock runs from two different starting points depending on the record type -- from creation or receipt of the record for the general category, or from the date of the employment action for personnel files of applicants or terminated employees -- and this clause does not resolve which starting point applies to any specific record.

WHAT RECORDS ARE COVERED: APPLICATIONS, PERSONNEL FILES, AND EMPLOYMENT REFERRAL RECORDS
The same statutory text that sets the four-year duration also defines what it reaches. Government Code § 12946(a) names the covered categories by name: applications, personnel records, membership records, and employment referral records and files -- for any employer, labor organization, or employment agency subject to FEHA -- and separately names personnel files of applicants or terminated employees. For a job applicant specifically, this covers the application itself, resume and any submitted supporting materials, and records generated during Acme, Inc.'s hiring process concerning that applicant, whether Acme, Inc. ultimately hired the applicant or not.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It shall be an unlawful practice for employers, labor organizations, and employment agencies subject to the provisions of this part to fail to maintain and preserve any and all applications, personnel, membership, or employment referral records and files for a minimum period of four years after the records and files are initially created or received, or for employers to fail to retain personnel files of applicants or terminated employees for a minimum period of four years after the date of the employment action taken."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12946.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause quotes the same subdivision, § 12946(a), already quoted in this document's duration clause -- it is the same source used a second time to address a distinct question (scope, not duration), not a second independent authority for the point. The statute does not itself define terms like "personnel records" or "employment referral records" beyond naming them; whether a specific document -- for example, an interviewer's informal notes, or a message exchanged with a staffing agency -- falls within one of these named categories is a characterization this clause does not resolve.

A FILED COMPLAINT EXTENDS THE RETENTION PERIOD UNTIL FINAL DISPOSITION
The four-year period is a floor, not a fixed endpoint. Government Code § 12946(b) provides that once an employer, labor organization, or employment agency has notice that a verified complaint has been filed against it under FEHA, it must maintain and preserve all records and files -- not only those relating to the specific complainant -- until the later of two dates: the first date after the time for filing a civil action has expired, or the first date after the complaint has been fully and finally disposed of and all administrative proceedings, civil actions, appeals, or related proceedings have terminated. For Acme, Inc., notice of a verified complaint under FEHA extends the applicable retention obligation past the routine four-year period for as long as that complaint, and any resulting proceedings, remain unresolved.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Upon notice that a verified complaint against it has been filed under this part, any such employer, labor organization, or employment agency shall maintain and preserve any and all records and files until the later of the following: (1) The first date after the period of time for filing a civil action has expired. (2) The first date after the complaint has been fully and finally disposed of and all administrative proceedings, civil actions, appeals, or related proceedings have terminated."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12946.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause is drawn from a single statutory subdivision, § 12946(b); no additional independent source was sought for this point. The subdivision's text extends the duty to "any and all records and files" once notice of a verified complaint is received, without limiting that duty to records connected to the specific complaint -- this clause states that scope as written, without resolving how it interacts in practice with unrelated records the employer may routinely destroy on other schedules. The statute also does not address what happens if a verified complaint is filed after records that predate it, and that would otherwise have fallen due for destruction, have already been lawfully destroyed under the routine four-year rule -- that scenario is not addressed in this clause.

THE FEDERAL BASELINE IS SHORTER: ONE YEAR UNDER EEOC REGULATIONS, TWO FOR MOST FEDERAL CONTRACTORS
Federal law imposes its own, separate recordkeeping duty on employers covered by Title VII, and it is shorter than California's. An EEOC regulation, 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14, requires that any personnel or employment record made or kept by a covered employer -- including application forms submitted by applicants and other records having to do with hiring -- be preserved for one year from the date the record is made or the personnel action occurs, whichever is later; for an involuntary termination, the terminated employee's personnel records must be kept for one year from the date of termination. That same federal regulation contains its own complaint-filing extension, parallel to California's: where a charge of discrimination has been filed, or an action brought by the EEOC or the Attorney General, against the employer under Title VII, the ADA, or GINA, the employer must preserve all personnel records relevant to the charge or action until its final disposition. A separate federal regulation applies a longer period to certain federal contractors: 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) requires a covered contractor to preserve personnel or employment records -- expressly including applications and resumes -- for not less than two years, or one year if the contractor has fewer than 150 employees or does not hold a government contract of at least $150,000.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any personnel or employment record made or kept by an employer (including but not necessarily limited to requests for reasonable accommodation, application forms submitted by applicants and other records having to do with hiring, promotion, demotion, transfer, lay-off or termination, rates of pay or other terms of compensation, and selection for training or apprenticeship) shall be preserved by the employer for a period of one year from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later."
  — 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14 (Cornell LII e-CFR text), 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/1602.14)
  "Any personnel or employment record made or kept by the contractor shall be preserved by the contractor for a period of not less than two years from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later. However, if the contractor has fewer than 150 employees or does not have a Government contract of at least $150,000, the minimum record retention period shall be one year from the date of the making of the record or the personnel action involved, whichever occurs later."
  — 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) (Cornell LII e-CFR text), 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/41/60-1.12)
  Known gap: These are two independent federal regulations issued by two different agencies for two different purposes -- 29 C.F.R. § 1602.14 (EEOC, applying to employers generally covered by Title VII, the ADA, and GINA) and 41 C.F.R. § 60-1.12(a) (OFCCP, applying specifically to covered federal contractors and subcontractors) -- not two subsections of the same regulation. This clause does not address every other record-retention rule that could separately apply to a given employer's hiring records -- for example, the federal Form I-9 retention rule, which this project's separate documents already cover -- nor does it determine whether a given employer meets the size or contract-value thresholds that would make the federal contractor regulation, rather than the general EEOC regulation, apply to it.

CALIFORNIA'S LONGER PERIOD CONTROLS FOR A CALIFORNIA EMPLOYER -- A FLOOR, NOT A CEILING
Where California's four-year retention period and the shorter one-year (or, for some federal contractors, two-year) federal period both apply to the same employer, the two periods are not alternatives that let an employer choose the shorter one -- they function as a floor and ceiling, with the longer period actually controlling. Title VII contains its own savings clause on this point: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 provides that nothing in Title VII "shall be deemed to exempt or relieve any person from any liability, duty, penalty, or punishment provided by any present or future law of any State," except a state law that purports to require or permit conduct that Title VII itself makes an unlawful employment practice. California's longer retention requirement does not require or permit anything Title VII forbids -- it requires more retention, not less -- so satisfying only the shorter federal period does not relieve Acme, Inc. of the separate, longer duty California law imposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Nothing in this subchapter shall be deemed to exempt or relieve any person from any liability, duty, penalty, or punishment provided by any present or future law of any State or political subdivision of a State, other than any such law which purports to require or permit the doing of any act which would be an unlawful employment practice under this subchapter."
  — 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 (Cornell LII text), 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/2000e-7)
  Known gap: 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-7 is a general non-preemption (savings) provision addressing Title VII's relationship to state law broadly; it is not a court decision or agency guidance applying that provision specifically to the two record-retention regulations described elsewhere in this document, and no such case law or agency guidance was independently verified this session. This clause states the general floor/ceiling principle those texts support; it does not address whether some other, more specific federal statute -- outside Title VII -- could expressly preempt a state recordkeeping duty in a way this general savings clause would not reach, a question this document does not attempt to resolve.

ENFORCEMENT: GOV. CODE § 12946 AUTHORIZES JUDICIAL RELIEF, NOT A STATED RECORDKEEPING PENALTY
Government Code § 12946 itself does not state a specific dollar penalty for an employer's failure to retain the records it covers. What the statute provides instead, in subdivisions (c) and (d), is rulemaking and enforcement authority: the (now Civil Rights) council is directed to adopt suitable rules, regulations, and standards to carry out the purposes of the section, and, where necessary, the department may, under its separate powers, seek temporary or preliminary judicial relief to enforce the section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "The council shall adopt suitable rules, regulations, and standards to carry out the purposes of this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(c)-(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12946.)
  "Where necessary, the department, pursuant to its powers under Section 12974, may seek temporary or preliminary judicial relief to enforce this section."
  — Cal. Gov. Code § 12946(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Government Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=12946.)
  Known gap: This is California's own statute, used as evidence of California's own enforcement mechanism -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific employer. This clause is drawn from a single statutory section's remaining subdivisions, § 12946(c) and (d); no additional independent source was sought for this point. Unlike some other California recordkeeping statutes -- for example, Labor Code § 1198.5, covered in this project's separate personnel-records-request document, which states a specific $750 penalty for noncompliance -- § 12946 does not itself state a comparable penalty for a retention failure. Disclosed honestly: this document does not assert that a missing record produces any particular evidentiary consequence, such as an adverse inference, in a later discrimination proceeding -- no case law or regulation establishing such a rule specific to this statute was fetched and confirmed against a primary source this session, so no such claim is made here.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF POLICY
Acme, Inc. has reviewed and adopted the record-retention policy for job application materials, resumes, and related hiring records described in this information sheet, effective October 1, 2026.

Company representative: _________________________
Title: _________________________
Date: October 1, 2026
Location: San Francisco, California

[This information sheet states facts about California and federal record-retention law as of the date checked above. It is not legal advice about any specific record, applicant, employee, or proceeding, and it does not itself extend, shorten, or waive any retention period that federal or California law separately requires.]
